topics.title: Air mass classification and source regions
lesson: An air mass is a large body of air, with horizontal dimensions of several hundred to a couple of thousand miles (Penn State) and fairly uniform temperature and moisture in the horizontal, but not in the vertical. It takes on the character of the region where it sits for an extended period (the source region). A uniform surface, light winds and a stable high-pressure pattern are the classic conditions (not confirmed).

list: By latitude: Arctic (A), Polar (P), Tropical (T).
By surface: continental (c, dry) or maritime (m, moist).
Combined: cA, cP, mP, cT, mT. Arctic air is usually continental.
cA: the coldest and driest air masses. Sources include Siberia and northern Canada (Penn State).
cP: forms over cold land and has low dew points. Canada is the most common source for North America (Penn State). Very cold, dry and stable at the source in winter.
mP: forms over high-latitude cold water (North Atlantic and North Pacific). Chilly and moist, with dew points close to the air temperature. Can bring fog to coastal New England (Penn State).
mT: Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean and the tropical western Atlantic. Warm and humid, with high dew points.
cT: southwestern US and northern Mexico (deserts). Hot and dry.

lesson: As an air mass moves, it changes. Cold air moving over a warmer surface (k, cold-type) heats from below and becomes unstable: cumuliform cloud, showers, good visibility. Warm air moving over a colder surface (w, warm-type) cools from below and becomes stable: stratus, fog, poor visibility.

lesson.note: Think about the surface the air is crossing. Cold over warm = unstable and showery. Warm over cold = stable and foggy.

terms: Area where an air mass acquires its temperature and moisture characteristics.
Moist (formed over water) / dry (formed over land).
Change in an air mass's properties as it moves away from its source.

questions.q: What are the characteristics of continental polar (cP) air at its source?
questions.e: cP forms over cold land, with Canada the most common North American source, and has low dew points.

questions.q: Which air mass source region produces warm, humid air for Atlantic Canada's summer thunderstorms?
questions.e: Maritime tropical air from the Gulf of Mexico and the western Atlantic is warm and moist.

questions.q: What happens when cold air flows over a warmer surface?
c: It becomes unstable, with cumuliform cloud and showers
It becomes stable, with stratus cloud and fog banks
It stays unchanged because air masses never modify
It dries out completely and produces cloud-free skies
questions.e: Heating from below steepens the lapse rate and promotes convection.

questions.q: What happens when warm moist air flows over a colder surface?
c: It becomes stable, with stratus and fog
questions.e: Cooling from below creates a stable layer where stratus and fog form.

questions.q: What does the 'm' in mP indicate?
questions.e: m means maritime (moist). mP is cool, moist polar air from oceans.

questions.q: Which air mass symbol describes cold, dry air formed over northern Canada in winter?
questions.e: Continental polar air forms over cold land and is cold and dry.

questions.q: A maritime tropical air mass moving over the Maritimes in summer typically brings:
c: Warm, humid air with fog, stratus or thunderstorms
Cold, dry air with clear skies and strong radiation inversions
Strong subsidence, a dry atmosphere and unlimited visibility
Arctic outflow with blowing snow and very cold temperatures
questions.e: mT air carries abundant warm moisture from the subtropical Atlantic.

questions.q: A cold air mass moves over a warmer surface and is heated from below. The air mass is called:
questions.e: A 'k' air mass is colder than the surface beneath it, so it tends to be unstable.

questions.q: Which source region characteristic makes an air mass uniform?
c: A large, flat area with light winds and uniform surface
A mountainous region with strong winds and many different surfaces
A narrow coastal strip with changing winds between land and sea
A region crossed by many fronts and frequent cyclones
questions.e: Air mass properties come from long residence over a uniform surface.

questions.q: Arctic air (A) differs from continental polar air mainly in being:
c: Colder, from the Arctic basin or ice-covered regions
Warmer and more humid, forming over the warm Gulf Stream
Formed only over the ocean, carrying large amounts of moisture
Associated with the subtropical high near 30 degrees latitude
questions.e: Arctic air comes from ice-covered high latitudes and is the coldest air mass type.

questions.q: Which statement about modification of an air mass is true?
c: It changes as it moves over surfaces unlike its source region
It never changes while it travels, whatever surface lies below it
It changes only in summer, when the surface is warm
It changes only when it crosses a mountain range or a coast
questions.e: Heating, cooling and moisture exchange with the new surface modify the air mass.

sources: Penn State METEO 3, Air masses and fronts: size, uniformity, five types (cA, cP, mP, cT, mT) and their North American source regions
Prof. Jin-Yi Yu, ESS 5 Chapter 9: classification symbols; mA does not exist
unverified: Modification (k and w types) and the stability changes they cause: standard teaching, not covered on the pages read.
Effects on the Maritimes (cloud, showers, thunderstorms) were removed or left unconfirmed; the sources are US course texts, not Canadian publications.
No ECCC page on air mass types was found.

topics.title: Cold, warm, stationary and occluded fronts
lesson: A front is the boundary between two air masses of different density. Fronts are named for the air that is advancing.

list: Warm air advances and rides up over retreating cold air along a gentle slope (about 1:200). Warm fronts move slowly, about 20 km/h.
Cloud lowers in sequence: Ci, Cs, As, Ns. Cirrus can appear about 1,000 km ahead and altostratus about 500 km ahead (Oklahoma Mesonet). Wide area of steady rain or snow ahead of the surface front.
Fog and freezing rain are possible ahead of the front.
After passage: warmer, winds veer (for example from southeast to south or southwest), pressure steadies.
Cold air advances and wedges under warm air on a steeper slope (about 1:100). Cold fronts move faster, up to about 50 km/h.
Narrow belt of showers, thunderstorms, gusty winds and squalls at or just ahead of the front.
After passage: temperature falls, pressure rises, wind veers (for example from southwest to northwest), skies clear and visibility improves.
Stationary front: neither air mass advances. Wind flows parallel to the front. Long periods of cloud and rain are possible.

Occluded front: a cold front overtakes a warm front, lifting the warm air off the surface. In North America the cold occlusion is the most common type. A cold occlusion has the coldest air behind; a warm occlusion has air behind that is warmer than the air ahead of the warm front.

lesson.note: Northern Hemisphere: winds typically veer (turn clockwise) with the passage of a warm or cold front.

terms: Boundary where warm air replaces cold air.
Boundary where cold air replaces warm air.
Front formed when a cold front overtakes a warm front.

questions.q: Which front has the shallower slope and a wider area of cloud and precipitation?
questions.e: Warm fronts slope about 1:200, spreading cloud and precipitation over a large area ahead of the surface line.

questions.q: What changes accompany the passage of a cold front in the Northern Hemisphere?
c: Temperature falls, pressure rises, wind veers
Temperature rises, pressure falls, wind backs
Temperature rises, pressure rises, wind backs
questions.e: Colder, denser air arrives, pressure rises, and the wind turns clockwise (for example SW to NW).

questions.q: What weather is typical along a fast-moving cold front?
c: A narrow band of showers, thunderstorms and squalls
A wide shield of steady drizzle and low stratus cloud
A broad area of fog with very light winds throughout
Several hundred kilometres of continuous steady snow ahead
questions.e: The steeper slope gives vigorous lifting and convection in a narrow zone.

questions.q: How does an occluded front form?
c: A cold front overtakes a warm front
questions.e: Cold fronts move faster than warm fronts and eventually catch up, lifting the warm air aloft.

questions.q: Which cloud sequence is associated with the approach of a warm front?
c: Nimbostratus, altostratus, cirrostratus, cirrus, clear sky
questions.e: Cloud thickens and lowers as the warm front approaches.

questions.q: The wind shifts from southwest to northwest, temperature drops and pressure rises sharply. What passed?
questions.e: Wind veer, falling temperature and rising pressure mark a cold front passage.

questions.q: Which front typically moves slower than the other, with gentle slope and widespread stratiform cloud?
questions.e: A warm front slopes at roughly 1:200 and brings layered cloud ahead of it.

questions.q: A stationary front is a boundary that:
questions.e: Neither air mass is replacing the other along a stationary front.

questions.q: In a cold occlusion, the air behind the cold front is:
c: Colder than the air ahead of the warm front
Warmer than the air ahead of the warm front
Equal in temperature to the air ahead
questions.e: In a cold occlusion the colder air undercuts the cool air ahead of the warm front.

questions.q: On a surface analysis a cold front is drawn with:
c: Purple line with triangles and semicircles
questions.e: Cold fronts are blue with triangles pointing in the direction of motion.

questions.q: Typical speeds quoted for fronts are:
c: Cold fronts up to about 50 km/h, warm fronts about 20 km/h
Cold fronts about 20 km/h, warm fronts up to about 50 km/h
questions.e: University of Alberta EAS 270 and Yu (ESS 5): warm fronts about 20 km/h, cold fronts up to 50 km/h.

questions.q: What cold front slope do several sources give as typical?
questions.e: Oklahoma Mesonet and Yu quote 1:100 for a typical cold front and 1:200 for a warm front.

sources: NWS Weather Prediction Center, Surface fronts and boundaries: cold front blue triangles, warm front red semicircles, occluded front purple triangles and semicircles
Oklahoma Mesonet, Fronts: slopes 1:100 and 1:200, cloud sequence distances, cold-type occlusion most common, stationary front behaviour
University of Alberta EAS 270 lecture 22 and Prof. Yu ESS 5: speeds, warm front freezing rain, cold front passage changes
unverified: Weather and wind changes after warm front passage (veering to south or southwest, pressure steadying): not stated on the pages read.
Warm occlusion description and the stationary front symbol: not on the pages read.
The earlier slope of 1:50 for cold fronts was removed; sources give about 1:100 (the University of Alberta slide marks it tentative).

topics.title: Frontal cross-sections and associated weather
lesson: A cross-section shows the cold air as a wedge under the warm air. The sloping boundary is the frontal surface. Friction slows the cold air near the ground, so the front is steepest near the surface (a nose).

list: Warm front: cloud shield extends hundreds of km ahead of the surface front. Steady precipitation covers a large area.
Cold front: active weather is usually a narrow belt along and just ahead of the front (a 50 to 100 km width was not confirmed). Squall lines can accompany cold fronts.
Ana cold front: warm air rises along the frontal surface. Wide cloud and precipitation extend behind the surface front.
Kata cold front: warm air descends. Weather is weak or confined to a narrow zone.

lesson: At the frontal surface, temperature increases with height as you pass from cold into warm air. This frontal inversion traps cloud, fog and pollutants in the cold air beneath.

list: Freezing rain: warm air overrunning sub-freezing air at the surface, typical of warm fronts and stationary fronts in winter.
Turbulence and wind shear across the frontal surface, especially with fast fronts.
Low ceiling and visibility in the cold air mass: fog, stratus, drizzle.

lesson.note: Any time a sounding shows a warm layer above 0 C over a sub-freezing layer at the ground, expect freezing rain or ice pellets.

terms: Sloping boundary between two air masses.
Temperature inversion at the boundary where warm air overlies cold air.
Fronts with rising / sinking warm air.

questions.q: Which front type commonly produces the widest precipitation shield?
questions.e: The shallow slope of the warm front lifts air gradually over a wide area.

questions.q: In an ana cold front, warm air:
questions.e: Ana means ascending; cloud and rain extend behind the surface front.

questions.q: What is the typical hazard when warm air overruns sub-freezing air at the ground?
questions.e: Rain falls through the cold surface layer and freezes on contact.

questions.q: A frontal inversion is:
c: Temperature increasing with height across the frontal surface
Temperature decreasing with height across the frontal surface
A pressure rise behind a front
questions.e: Passing from cold air to warm air above produces an inversion at the front.

questions.q: Where is the active weather of a fast-moving cold front typically concentrated?
c: Near and just ahead of the front
Far ahead in a wide shield
questions.e: Steep frontal slope concentrates lifting into a narrow band.

questions.q: Which cloud sequence is typical ahead of an approaching warm front?
c: Cumulonimbus then cirrus then clear sky with gusty winds
Stratus first, then cirrus, then fair-weather cumulus
Altocumulus lenticularis, then cirrus, then clear sky
questions.e: Warm frontal lifting progressively lowers the cloud base.

questions.q: Which weather is typical right behind a fast-moving cold front in winter?
c: Gusty northwest winds, flurries and rapidly clearing sky
Steady warm-sector drizzle with low stratus and poor visibility
Dense fog and calm winds with a falling temperature
Widespread freezing rain falling from altostratus cloud
questions.e: Cold post-frontal air brings gusts and scattered convective cloud.

questions.q: The slope of a typical cold front is steeper than a warm front's. This leads to:
c: No difference in the width of weather
Weather only after the front passes
questions.e: A steeper slope concentrates lifting in a narrow zone.

questions.q: Freezing rain ahead of a warm front requires:
c: A warm layer aloft over a shallow sub-zero layer at the surface
A deep layer of cold air from the ground up to 5 km
Dry air with no cloud and a strong surface inversion
A surface temperature above 5 C with rain reaching the ground
questions.e: Snow melts in the warm layer and freezes on contact below.

questions.q: The warm sector of a mid-latitude cyclone lies:
c: Between the cold and warm fronts
At the centre of the occlusion
questions.e: The warm sector is the wedge of warm air between the two fronts.

questions.q: Which phenomenon is a typical hazard to aviation at a warm front?
c: Low ceilings and poor visibility in widespread precipitation
Only clear-air turbulence, with no cloud or precipitation at all
Severe thunderstorms and tornadoes in every case
Dust storms and very strong winds with unlimited visibility
questions.e: Warm fronts bring low stratus, rain or snow and poor visibility over a wide area.

sources: Oklahoma Mesonet, Fronts and Yu ESS 5: warm front cloud shield and stratiform weather, cold front squall lines, freezing rain with warm fronts
unverified: Frontal cross-section details (nose near the surface), ana and kata fronts, and the frontal inversion: standard teaching, not on the pages read.
Width of the cold front weather band (50 to 100 km): removed as unconfirmed.
Weather behind a cold front in winter: standard teaching.

topics.title: Frontogenesis and frontolysis
lesson: Fronts are not permanent. They form, strengthen, weaken and disappear.

list: Frontogenesis: formation or strengthening of a front, meaning an increase in the horizontal temperature gradient.
Frontolysis: weakening or dissipation of a front, meaning a decrease in the temperature gradient.

Horizontal confluence in a deformation field: air from warm and cold sides is squeezed together. NWS: the flow is frontogenetic when the isotherms lie within 45 degrees of the axis of dilatation, and frontolytic beyond 45 degrees.
Horizontal wind shear alone only rotates the isotherms and does not change the gradient (NWS), so it matters when combined with deformation.
Differential vertical motion (tilting), which can strengthen or weaken the horizontal gradient.
Differential heating (diabatic), for example cloud cover warming one air mass faster than the other.

lesson: Frontolysis happens when the air flow becomes diffluent (spreading), when the temperature difference is mixed away, or when the front moves over a surface that evens out temperatures.

In winter, the east coast of North America is a frontogenesis zone: cold continental air meets the relatively warm Gulf Stream. The strong baroclinic zone there supports rapid storm development that affects Atlantic Canada.

Baroclinic air has horizontal temperature gradients, with surfaces of constant pressure and density intersecting. Fronts and jet streams exist in baroclinic zones. Barotropic air has no horizontal temperature gradient on pressure surfaces.

lesson.note: No temperature gradient, no front. Anything that sharpens the gradient makes frontogenesis.

terms: Intensification of a horizontal temperature gradient to form or strengthen a front.
Region with strong horizontal temperature gradient.

questions.q: What is frontogenesis?
c: Formation or strengthening of a front
Movement of a front over mountains
questions.e: Frontogenesis sharpens the horizontal temperature gradient.

questions.q: Which wind pattern favours frontogenesis?
c: Confluence that squeezes warm and cold air together
Diffluence that spreads warm and cold air farther apart
Calm winds with no horizontal variation across the region
Vertical sinking over a large area without any horizontal flow
questions.e: Confluent flow along the axis of dilatation concentrates temperature contrasts.

questions.q: A baroclinic atmosphere is one where:
c: There are horizontal temperature gradients on pressure surfaces
Temperature is uniform in the horizontal on all pressure surfaces
Wind speed is constant with height at every point in the column
Pressure is the same everywhere on each constant-height surface
questions.e: Baroclinic conditions go with fronts and jet streams.

questions.q: What is frontolysis?
c: Weakening or dissipation of a front
questions.e: Lysis means dissolving; the temperature gradient decreases.

questions.q: Why is the US east coast a favoured area for winter frontogenesis?
c: Cold continental air meets the warm Gulf Stream waters
Mountains in the region block the cold air from reaching the coast
Tropical cyclones form there every month and create frontal zones
Ocean and land temperatures are the same, producing uniform air masses
questions.e: The strong land-sea temperature contrast sharpens the gradient.

questions.q: Frontogenesis refers to:
c: The formation or strengthening of a front
The movement of a front over mountains
questions.e: Frontogenesis intensifies the temperature gradient.

questions.q: Convergence of flow with a temperature gradient across the flow causes:
questions.e: Confluence squeezes isotherms together and strengthens the gradient.

questions.q: Diffluent flow over a front typically leads to:
questions.e: Diffluence spreads isotherms apart and weakens the front.

questions.q: Where do fronts often become more active?
c: Where a jet stream or upper trough provides lift
Under a strong surface high with sinking air and clear skies
Under a subsidence inversion in light winds and clear air
Over a calm, cold sea with a shallow stable layer
questions.e: Upper-level support enhances vertical motion along the front.

questions.q: An analyst sees tightly packed isotherms across a frontal zone. This indicates:
questions.e: Close isotherms mean a large change in temperature over a short distance.

questions.q: Frontolysis commonly occurs when:
c: A front moves into a region with a weak temperature contrast
A front meets a strong thermal gradient and a converging flow
A trough deepens quickly and pulls cold air toward the front
A jet stream strengthens over the front and adds upper lift
questions.e: A weakening gradient means the front fades.

questions.q: Per NWS, the flow is frontogenetic when the angle between the isotherms and the axis of dilatation is:
c: It does not depend on the angle
questions.e: NWS: under 45 degrees is frontogenetic; over 45 degrees is frontolytic.

questions.q: On its own, horizontal shear (pure vorticity) does what to the isotherms?
c: Rotates them without changing the gradient
Squeezes them together to strengthen the front
Spreads them apart to weaken the front
questions.e: NWS: pure vorticity acts to rotate isotherms and does not change the gradient's magnitude.

sources: NWS Louisville, Frontogenesis: definition, deformation and the 45 degree rule, shear, tilting, diabatic heating
EUMETRAIN, Meteorological physical background: deformation as a primary factor; frontogenesis strongest in the confluence zone
unverified: Baroclinic and barotropic definitions, and the winter frontogenesis zone off the US east coast where cold air meets the Gulf Stream: standard teaching, not on the pages read.
Which mechanisms cause frontolysis besides diffluence (mixing away, moving over an even surface): not confirmed.
Upper jet or trough supporting front activity: not confirmed.
